LEARN MORE » Sections বাংলা Monday, November 23, 2026 Today's Paper Video e-Paper Second Edition Contact Sections Home Frontpage Asia City World OP-ED Editorial Business Global Business Commercial Capital Sports Countrywide Featured Sex & Relationship Student Voice LitScape Life Style Reciprocal Teens & Twenties In Vogue Food & Nutrition Bookshelf Entertainment Back Page × Home World Published: 10:23 PM, 21 November 2026 Ethiopia, Sudan Accuse One Another of Backing Armed Groups AA News Desk Tensions between Ethiopia and Sudan have escalated sharply as the two neighboring countries accuse each other of supporting armed groups fighting within their respective territories. The growing diplomatic dispute has raised fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa, a strategically important region already struggling with political instability, civil wars, humanitarian emergencies, and competing regional interests. Analysts warn that continued hostility between Addis Ababa and Khartoum could transform their internal conflicts into a dangerous regional confrontation. The latest tensions have emerged against the backdrop of Sudan's devastating civil war, which began in April 2023, and renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Both countries have accused the other of providing assistance to armed opponents, including military training, logistical support, access to territory, and other forms of cooperation. However, both governments have rejected the allegations made against them, and the claims have not been independently verified. Sudan's military leadership has accused Ethiopia of allowing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), to establish camps on Ethiopian territory. According to Sudanese officials, Ethiopian territory has allegedly been used to facilitate drone operations and cross-border attacks against Sudanese positions and infrastructure. Khartoum considers such activities a direct threat to its national security and territorial sovereignty. In early November 2026, Sudan's military authorities submitted formal complaints against Ethiopia to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council. They claimed to have provided evidence supporting their allegations. The diplomatic move demonstrated the seriousness of Sudan's concerns and its determination to seek international attention regarding the alleged involvement of its eastern neighbor. Ethiopia, however, has strongly rejected the accusations and made counterclaims against Sudan. Addis Ababa alleges that the Sudanese military is supporting armed rebels operating in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fighting resumed there in September 2026, threatening the peace agreement signed in Pretoria in 2022, which had brought an end to the devastating conflict between Ethiopian federal forces and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Ethiopian military leaders have also accused Sudan, Eritrea, and Egypt of supporting opposition groups seeking to destabilize the country. These allegations have been rejected by the countries concerned. The Ethiopian government maintains that external interference is contributing to its domestic security challenges. The diplomatic confrontation has already produced tangible consequences. In early November, Ethiopia closed the Sudanese consulate in the border town of Asosa and ordered six Sudanese diplomatic staff members to leave the country. Sudan subsequently closed the Ethiopian consulate in Gedaref and expelled its diplomatic personnel. The reciprocal actions marked a further deterioration in relations and reduced opportunities for direct diplomatic communication between the two governments. Several historical and political disputes have contributed to the worsening relationship. One major issue is the disputed Al-Fashaga border region, a fertile agricultural area claimed by both countries. Ethiopian farmers have traditionally cultivated parts of the territory, while Sudan has repeatedly asserted its sovereignty over the region. In late 2020, Sudanese troops moved into the disputed area as Ethiopian forces were engaged in fighting in Tigray. The disagreement has remained a significant source of tension. Another important issue is the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), constructed on the Blue Nile River in Ethiopia. Although the dam is expected to strengthen Ethiopia's electricity generation capacity and support economic development, Sudan and Egypt have expressed concerns about its impact on downstream water resources. The absence of a comprehensive, legally binding agreement on the dam's operation and water management has further complicated regional relations. The involvement of external powers has also made the situation more complicated. Different countries have developed competing political and security partnerships across the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia has maintained important relationships with the United Arab Emirates, while Sudan has developed closer ties with Egypt and Eritrea. Turkey has also maintained relations with both countries. These overlapping alliances could make regional diplomacy more difficult if the confrontation intensifies. The humanitarian consequences of the two countries' internal conflicts are already devastating. Sudan's war has killed at least 59,000 people, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, while approximately 13 million people have been displaced. Millions more face food shortages, inadequate medical facilities, and limited access to essential services. Renewed fighting in Ethiopia could create another wave of displacement and place additional pressure on humanitarian organizations. For Bangladesh and other developing countries, instability in the Horn of Africa deserves attention because regional conflicts can disrupt international trade, maritime transportation, energy markets, and global supply chains. The Horn of Africa occupies an important geographical position near the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, through which substantial volumes of international commerce pass. A wider military confrontation could create additional security and economic challenges for countries dependent on international trade. The international community, particularly the United Nations and the African Union, should take urgent diplomatic initiatives to prevent further escalation. Both Ethiopia and Sudan must respect each other's sovereignty and refrain from supporting armed groups operating across international borders. Independent investigations into the allegations could help establish the facts and reduce mutual suspicion. Regular diplomatic communication, confidence-building measures, and peaceful border management are also essential. Ultimately, Ethiopia and Sudan cannot achieve lasting security through mutual accusations and military confrontation. Both countries face serious domestic challenges that require political reconciliation, economic recovery, and humanitarian assistance. Their governments should recognize that regional cooperation is far more beneficial than prolonged hostility. Preventing another major conflict in the Horn of Africa is not only a responsibility of Ethiopia and Sudan but also an important concern for the entire international community. Peaceful dialogue, mutual respect, and adherence to international law remain the best ways to protect regional stability and promote a more secure future. This diplomatic dispute raises concerns about a potential wider conflict in the politically unstable Horn of Africa. Sudan's military has alleged that Ethiopia is harboring the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which are engaged in a civil war against Sudan's Armed Forces, claiming that Ethiopian territory is being used for military operations against Sudan. In response, Ethiopia has accused Sudan of backing rebels in its northern Tigray region, where fighting has resumed, threatening a previous peace agreement. The situation has led to reciprocal closures of consulates and expulsions of diplomatic staff, further straining relations. Historical disputes, particularly over the Al-Fashaga border region and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, complicate matters. The humanitarian impact is severe, with thousands dead and millions displaced, highlighting the urgent need for international diplomatic intervention to prevent further escalation and promote regional stability.

Report us Related Topics Ethiopia Climate change Addis Ababa From November 8 to 19, 2027, thousands of world leaders, climate negotiators, scientists and financiers will gather in Addis Ababa for 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32). Ethiopia has secured the presidency of the United Nations climate summit, a major diplomatic achievement that places the seat of the African Union at the center of global climate finance and renewable energy talks. Ethiopian officials have presented the event as proof of the country’s emergence as a green powerhouse, citing the Green Legacy reforestation campaign and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Africa’s largest hydroelectric facility. Gallery The security picture has deteriorated quickly. Forces loyal to Ethiopia’s federal government in Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, after recapturing the city from Tigrayan rebels on Oct. 4 ( Photo: Obtained by REUTERS ) Yet the same government is preparing for that spotlight while its neighborhood slides toward confrontation. Ethiopia’s greatest diplomatic success may become a practical constraint on its regional ambitions. Hosting COP32 creates reputational, financial and diplomatic incentives for restraint that Addis Ababa cannot easily ignore. Whether those incentives prove strong enough remains an open question with direct implications for Israel’s security along the Red Sea. The security picture has deteriorated quickly. Tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea escalated after fighting resumed between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan units in September 2026 and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations in response to Addis Ababa's decision to close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats. Troop concentrations near Badme, the flashpoint of the 1998–2000 war, have raised fears of direct confrontation. ACLED reported artillery exchanges and clashes near Badme on November 12 and 13, although Reuters could not independently verify direct fighting between the two armies. The African Union has called for restraint as the risk of wider fighting grows. Ethiopia’s long-standing search for sovereign Red Sea access compounds the problem. The 2024 memorandum with Somaliland triggered sharp opposition from Somalia, which views any arrangement that challenges its territorial integrity as unacceptable. Subsequent diplomacy produced the Ankara Declaration of December 11, 2024. Under that Turkish-facilitated agreement, Ethiopia and Somalia committed to negotiate reliable Ethiopian sea access under Somali sovereignty. The original memorandum created a crisis. The later framework established a different, still fragile path. Progress remains limited and distrust persists on both sides. These disputes have drawn in other regional actors. The October 4 El Alamein Declaration brought Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia together around sovereignty, territorial integrity and regional stability. The text affirms that Red Sea governance belongs to littoral states and rejects unilateral Nile measures that harm downstream countries. It also calls for peaceful solutions and does not name Ethiopia as an adversary. Even so, the declaration functions as a strategic counterweight to Ethiopian influence in both the Nile Basin and the Red Sea corridor. Cairo’s decision to deepen this coordination under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi prioritizes pressure over mediation. Cairo's close coordination with Khartoum, Asmara and Mogadishu increases diplomatic pressure on Addis Ababa. Although the declaration invokes peaceful solutions, its coordination framework strengthens a regional alignment whose positions on Nile waters, Somaliland and Red Sea governance frequently clash with Ethiopian interests. Red Sea ( Photo: Konoplytska/Shutterstock ) The Sisi regime has long treated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as a national security issue. Its regional posture amplifies zero-sum competition rather than reducing it. Sudan adds another layer of friction. Khartoum accuses Addis Ababa of supporting the Rapid Support Forces. Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing Tigrayan rebels. Both sides deny the charges. With Sudan already engulfed in civil war, any spillover across the shared border would further destabilize the region and multiply the risks facing civilian populations already suffering from displacement and food shortages. A separate diplomatic rupture between Somalia and the United Arab Emirates has complicated the picture further. Mogadishu expelled the UAE ambassador and earlier canceled agreements on ports, defense and security cooperation. Abu Dhabi rejected the accusations as escalatory. Because Gulf states maintain deep stakes in Red Sea ports and security arrangements, the dispute feeds uncertainty that reaches Addis Ababa’s own calculations. The Somalia-UAE confrontation remains secondary to the core state rivalries, yet it illustrates how quickly bilateral disputes can unsettle an already tense environment. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of these risks. It links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and carries a significant share of global maritime traffic. Any expansion of interstate conflict or further fragmentation of Somalia’s security landscape would create openings for armed groups. Al-Shabaab and residual ISIS-linked networks already operate in the region. They do not require control of capitals to threaten shipping lanes or project violence. Iran-backed Houthi forces have separately demonstrated the ability to disrupt traffic through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb. These threats exist independently. Together they make instability in the Horn a direct concern for Israel. The Red Sea is a strategic corridor for Israel , connecting the region to Asian and East African trade while exposing its southern maritime approaches to hostile forces. Bank of Israel research found that maritime imports from Asia and Oceania amounted to approximately $20 billion in 2023, around one-fifth of Israel's civilian imports. Although shipping diversions following Houthi attacks did not significantly reduce Israeli imports, they demonstrated how instability around Bab el-Mandeb can force vessels onto substantially longer routes and complicate maritime security. A wider crisis in the Horn would expand the operational space available to radical networks whose activities already endanger open sea lanes. Egypt’s contribution under Sisi has been to reinforce competitive alignments rather than to lower temperatures. A foreign policy that prioritizes short-term pressure on Ethiopia is not a stabilizing force. It is a risk multiplier for every state that relies on a secure Red Sea, including Israel. This is the context in which COP32 becomes more than a climate conference. Hosting the summit places Ethiopia under sustained international scrutiny. Foreign ministries, development banks, corporate sponsors and security services will examine the host country’s stability, airspace safety and regional relationships. This scrutiny is already underway. A joint UNFCCC and UN security mission visited Addis Ababa in July 2026 to assess venue, accommodation, transport, security and health preparations. Discussions on the host-country agreement have also begun. Ethiopia cannot afford a full-scale regional war in the months leading to November 2027 without damaging the credibility, attendance and financial success of the event. Major delegations and private investors can revise their plans if northern Ethiopia descends into cross-border fighting or if regional tensions dominate the agenda. Climate vulnerability and political conflict reinforce each other across the Horn. Drought, erratic rainfall, food insecurity and displacement place additional strain on governments already managing internal wars and mutual suspicion. If Addis Ababa intends to present itself as a leader in climate adaptation and cross-border resilience, partners will expect evidence of cooperation closer to home. Ethiopia has already begun framing COP32 as an inclusive platform for dialogue and climate finance delivery. That positioning creates leverage. The summit cannot resolve territorial disputes or replace direct negotiations. It can, however, raise the cost of escalation. Reputational damage, delayed climate financing, postponed investment and diminished international standing are concrete risks. Those risks give Ethiopian decision-makers incentives for restraint that did not exist before the country won the right to host. The prestige of the summit and the economic stakes attached to it may yet encourage cooler calculations in Addis Ababa and among its neighbors in the months ahead. COP32 will not settle the Nile dispute, resolve Ethiopia's maritime ambitions or erase the grievances separating Addis Ababa from its neighbors. But it can make escalation more costly for a government seeking to present itself as a global climate leader. Ethiopia's real test is whether it can translate international prestige into restraint at home and diplomacy abroad. For Israel, the question is whether the states surrounding the Red Sea can contain their rivalries before armed groups and external powers exploit the resulting instability. Amine Ayoub, a fellow at the Middle East Forum, is a policy analyst and writer based in Morocco. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is facing escalating tensions with regional rivals Eritrea and Sudan, raising concerns about potential conflict ahead of the COP32 climate summit scheduled for November 2027 in Addis Ababa. As Ethiopia prepares to host this significant event, which aims to position the country as a leader in climate finance and renewable energy, the deteriorating security situation poses a challenge to its diplomatic ambitions. Recent clashes near the contested Badme region and strained relations with Eritrea have heightened fears of direct confrontation. Additionally, Ethiopia's quest for access to the Red Sea has sparked opposition from Somalia, complicating regional dynamics. The African Union has called for restraint, but the involvement of other nations, including Egypt and Sudan, adds pressure on Ethiopia. The COP32 summit could serve as a platform for dialogue, but it also places Ethiopia under international scrutiny, making it imperative for the government to manage regional tensions to ensure the event's success and maintain its credibility.

Opinion November 21, 2026 Updated: November 21, 2026 Why Ethiopia Has Not Found Peace — and How Ethiopians Can Build It November 21, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber An evidence-based analysis of conflict, governance, and pathways to a durable settlement Publication draft prepared for review and attribution by the intended publisher. This is an independent analytical draft, not an endorsement by any organization. The author (file photo) Aklog Birara (Dr) Executive summary Ethiopia’s experience since 2018 is not a simple story of a peace prize followed by war. It is a story of an initially promising opening that did not resolve deeper struggles over political legitimacy, The newly appointed Prime Minister of Ethiopia Abiy Ahmed Ali managed to do two things simultaneously: charmed Ethiopians and the international community presenting himself and his party as reformists; and b) dismantled national institutions systematically and replaced them with Oromo elites and beneficiaries. This state capture changed the distribution of power, income and wealth, security arrangements, identity, land, and accountability. By all measurements on the ground concerning human life and wellbeing, Abiy Ahmed Ali is a murderer/genocider. Bloodletting of civilians he considers unworthy of life does not bother him. He undermines peace and democracy deliberately and systematically. Abiy Ahmed Ali suffers from a distorted mindset of grievance redress by punishing his enemies and opponents, slaughtering, starving, displacing, harassing, jailing primarily Amhara and Tigrayans (Abyssinians or northerners) by any means necessary. The costs are enormous. Accountability matters Abiy Ahmed Ali and partners must be held accountable for war crimes, crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing. Ethiopia will never enjoy peace without accountability. The institutional and structural changes taking place under the watch of Abiy Ahmed Ali are dramatic and irreversible. Think of the replacement of Ethiopia with Oromia; think of the change in the redesignation of Addis Ababa as Finfinnee. Think of Afan Oromo replacing Amharic as Ethiopia’s official language. There is nothing the international community would do if these were to occur. The 2018 rapprochement with Eritrea was a genuine diplomatic achievement. Yet the 2020–22 Tigray war, continuing violence in Oromia and the conflict in Amhara since 2023 reveal how fragile a settlement becomes when adversaries do not trust institutions or believe they can protect their interests peacefully. Root causes remain intact. The 2022 Pretoria agreement stopped a major phase of warfare but did not settle all underlying disputes or include all directly affected constituencies. [1–5] A viable peace process must therefore do more than obtain another ceasefire. It needs enforceable civilian-protection commitments, inclusive negotiation, independent monitoring, credible justice, space for peaceful political competition, and a negotiated approach to contested constitutional and territorial questions. No community should have to accept collective punishment, and no armed actor including the ruling party should be exempt from scrutiny. The single most critical hurdle to lasting peace and stability in Ethiopia is the Abiy ruling party and state. It is intolerant of peace and stability. It thrives on division. conflict and war. It breeds animosity and fear among ethnic and faith groups. It compromises Ethiopia’s sovereign interests by submitting itself to the UAE and its regional national goals. How does one explain Abiy Ahmed’s strategic partnership with Sudan’ s RSF? With the UAE? Why peace is illusive in Ethiopia. From the promise of 2018 to recurrent conflict Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in April 2018 and initiated reforms, including political prisoner releases and an opening of civic space. The Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 recognized particularly his role in the rapprochement with Eritrea, not a finding that Ethiopia had achieved lasting internal peace. The Nobel committee itself acknowledged the difficulty of democratization and continuing internal conflicts. [1] The question posed to the Nobel Committee is why a peace prize without demonstrated commitment to permanent peace and democratization? The transition unfolded amid longstanding grievances over centralized authority, ethnically organized federalism, political exclusion, competing territorial claims and unequal perceptions of security. Conflict between the federal government and the TPLF escalated into war in November 2020. The war involved federal, Tigrayan, Eritrean and regional forces, and devastated communities across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. The African Union-mediated Pretoria cessation-of-hostilities agreement of November 2022 reduced the fighting but left disputes over territory, displacement, implementation, and accountability unresolved. [2, 3, 6] The AU failed to demand inclusion of critical stakeholders: Afar and Amhara. In Amhara, tensions over the Pretoria process, territorial claims, and the April 2023 plan to dismantle regional special forces contributed to a confrontation between federal forces and Fano formations. In Oromia, armed conflict involving the Oromo Liberation Army and government forces persisted, accompanied by allegations of serious abuses against civilians. These conflicts have different histories; treating them as one undifferentiated rebellion obscures what each settlement must address. [2, 4, 7] Left with a sense of impunity, the Abiy government continued its assaults on civilians in the Afar. Amhara, Gambella, Oromia, Somali and Tigray regions. The latest flare between Oromo and Somali regional forces with the complicity of federal forces forced tens of thousands to flee to Kenya. In effect, Abiy Ahmed’s war is no longer confined to the Amhara and Tigray regions . It is national and regional. What the evidence shows about the democratic deficit. Freedom House’s 2026 assessment classifies Ethiopia as “Not Free,” scoring it eighteen out of one hundred, and identifies restrictions on political competition, media, civil society, due process, and independent institutions. Its Freedom on the Net report identifies connectivity restrictions in conflict-affected areas, including Amhara. These are assessments by an independent monitoring organization, not a legal determination that every government action is unlawful. [4, 8] Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026 describes continued armed conflict, serious abuses by warring parties, and restrictions on civic space. The UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia documented serious violations and abuses by multiple parties during the northern war, including war crimes and crimes against humanity. Responsibility for incidents must still be assessed on evidence, with individual accountability rather than collective blame. [2, 5] 3 | Why peace has remained elusive: Competing claims of political legitimacy Many political constituencies disagree not only about who should govern but about the rules of the state itself: the balance of federal and regional authority, the rights of individuals and communities, the electoral system, and the status of disputed territories. Without trusted procedures for resolving those questions, every major policy dispute can become a security crisis. In huge part, the reason is because Abiy Ahmed Ali has Oromoized the state and government. Non-Oromo are subject to alienation, marginalization, and submission. The option left is to defend their sheer survival. Security dilemmas and coercive disarmament When communities fear that, surrendering arms leaves them vulnerable, disarmament without credible guarantees can intensify insecurity. Conversely, the proliferation of armed forces undermines civilian authority and exposes communities to abuse. Sequenced, independently verified security arrangements are essential; neither unconditional coercion nor indefinite militarization offers a stable solution. Incomplete peace agreements and excluded stakeholders Pretoria demonstrated that negotiation could stop large-scale fighting. It also illustrates the limits of a deal that does not settle implementation, return of displaced people, disputed boundaries, and the security concerns of other affected actors. Durable arrangements must incorporate local communities, women, displaced persons, and civil society—not only the signatories who command fighters. [3, 6] Pretoria is flawed because it is not inclusive. Impunity, civilian harm, and collapsing trust Allegations of unlawful killings, arbitrary detention, attacks on health care, abductions and abuses by both state and non-state actors deepen grievances and discourage reconciliation. Independent investigations, survivor-centered remedies, and fair trials are necessary to break cycles of retaliation. The absence of trusted justice also makes ceasefires difficult to sustain. [2, 5] Humanitarian distress and regional spillover Displacement, damaged health and education systems, insecurity along transport routes, and constraints on relief access compound the political crisis. Relations with Eritrea and Sudan and disputes across the Horn of Africa add external incentives and risks. A November 2026 U.S. A Congressional Research Service report warns that overlapping rebellions and regional tensions could fuel a wider confrontation; such risk analysis should not be confused with a prediction that war is inevitable. [3, 9] The United Arab Emirates is a major component of the Ethiopian crisis. The international community must sanction this state actor that supplies drones and other weapons to Abiy’s army that in turn uses these weapons to slaughter civilians like chickens. The UAE is a destabilizing force in Africa. Independent domestic and international observers question “ Why Ethiopian elites fail to work together, do the needful and propose viable solutions with a timeframe” is baffling. What Ethiopians together can do: a practical peace architecture. First 90 days: protect lives and create a credible opening. Announce and independently monitor reciprocal civilian-protection commitments: no attacks on civilians, schools, clinics, aid workers, or civilian infrastructure; publish incident-reporting channels and rapid investigation procedures. Negotiate localized humanitarian pauses and safe access routes, with UN, Red Cross and trusted Ethiopian relief organizations assessing needs impartially across Amhara, Oromia, Tigray, Afar and other affected areas. Begin confidential exploratory talks involving federal authorities and relevant armed and civilian representatives; establish mutually acceptable mediators and guarantees against retaliation for peaceful participation. Release people arbitrarily detained, protect journalists and civil society monitors, restore communications where restricted, and enable independent observation subject to lawful security safeguards. Three to twelve months: negotiate and verify. Create an inclusive national peace forum with meaningful participation by women, youth, religious leaders, professional associations, displaced communities, minority groups, and diaspora voices; participation must not be equated with endorsing any armed group. Agree on phased ceasefires and security arrangements, with transparent benchmarks for troop repositioning, demobilization, reintegration, local policing, and protection of vulnerable populations. Establish independent, survivor-centered mechanisms for documentation, truth-seeking, reparations and prosecution of serious crimes, with safeguards for witness security and due process. Launch technical commissions on contested territories, federal-regional powers, land rights, and electoral rules; defer final decisions to legitimate constitutional and democratic procedures rather than military victory. One to three years: institutionalize peace. Strengthen electoral administration, judicial independence, parliamentary oversight and protections for opposition parties, media, and civil society. Rebuild public services and livelihoods using transparent needs-based allocations, audited funds, and community oversight; prioritize displaced people’s voluntary, safe and dignified return, or other durable solutions. Develop shared civic education and cross-community dialogue that recognize the suffering of Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, Afar, Somali, and other Ethiopian civilians without competitive victimhood. Secure regional non-interference commitments and international support for verification and reconstruction, while keeping Ethiopian communities central to decisions. 5 | Who must contribute—and what they can commit to. Federal institutions: uphold constitutional and humanitarian obligations, enable independent monitoring, negotiate in good faith, and accept impartial accountability. Armed groups: halt attacks on civilians, permit humanitarian access, reject forced recruitment, and participate in verifiable security talks. Political parties and regional administrations: pursue claims through nonviolent, transparent processes. Religious and community leaders: provide trusted spaces for dialogue without silencing victims. Diaspora organizations: support documented advocacy, relief, and bridge-building rather than dehumanizing rhetorical hold vigils and protests and highlight the tragedy inflicted on ordinary citizens by their own government that is supposed to protect them. In this connection, the protests consisting of members of the Horn of Africa in Washington on November 16 as well as those in Minnesota that issued a strong statement calling on the international community to hold the government of Ethiopia accountable are remarkable and encouraging developments. International partners: support mediation, needs-based aid, and independent accountability without imposing a political outcome. How to measure whether a peace process is real Public monthly indicators should include civilian deaths and injuries independently documented; safe humanitarian access and assistance delivered; school and clinic functionality; verified ceasefire violations; numbers of displaced people accessing voluntary durable solutions; arbitrary detention cases reviewed; participation of women and displaced communities in talks; and implementation of agreed security and justice milestones. A peace announcement without measurable improvement in civilian safety is insufficient. Conclusions Abiy Ahmed’s OPDO dominance and reconfiguration of the Ethiopian State notwithstanding, Ethiopia’s crisis cannot be explained solely by one leader, one ethnicity or one-armed movement. It is the entire system that must be overhauled. Decisions by political and military leaders’ matter, but the deeper challenge is the absence of trusted, enforceable rules for resolving disagreement. The 2018 opening showed that change is possible; the wars that followed show that ethnic elite dominated diplomacy without inclusive institutions is fragile. Assessing and critiquing the OPDO-dominated Prosperity Party is important but not enough. Ethiopia cannot afford to suffer from a mental model of permanent war. It is not a win-win model at all. It is a choice Aby Ahmed has chosen, but not for the benefit and wellbeing of the Ethiopian people. Equally, the Amhara Fano National Movement has an obligation to assess its institutional and leadership strengths and weaknesses and renew itself. The leadership must also evaluate the value added of the newly formed Alliance for Survival. Whose agenda is this new entity advancing? Long-term Ethiopians can build a more durable peace by insisting on good and democratic governance that guarantees equal civilian protection, accountable government, nonviolent political competition, genuine representation, and practical agreements whose implementation can be verified. There is no evidence that the Abiy regime is ready and willing to democratize Ethiopia. The choice of constitutional arrangements and political leadership belongs to Ethiopians through peaceful, rights-respecting processes. This is the reason a Pan-Ethiopian platform to discuss the elephant in the room–why no peace and democracy? – is essential. Finally, this author believes Ethiopians together must push for an all-inclusive series of conferences at the earliest opportunity. Sources and editorial notes Nobel Peace Prize, “2019 — Abiy Ahmed Ali” https://www.nobelpeaceprize.org/laureates/2019 Human Rights Watch, World Report 2026: Ethiopia https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2026/country-chapters/ethiopia Congressional Research Service, The Unfolding Conflict in Ethiopia, November 6, 2026 https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2026-11-06_IF13344_c5a4aa38378990aa0f52cb314883fe9fc012dabe.pdf Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2026: Ethiopia https://freedomhouse.org/country/ethiopia/freedom-world/2026 UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, investigative findings (2023) https://www.un.org/sexualviolenceinconflict/wpcontent/uploads/2023/10/report/comprehensive-investigative-findings-and-legaldeterminations-international-commission-of-human-rights-experts-on-ethiopia/a-hrc-54crp-3.pdf UK Home Office, Country Policy, and Information Note: Tigrayans and TPLF (December 2024) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ethiopia-country-policy-and-informationnotes/country-policy-and-information-note-tigrayans-and-the-tigrayan-peoples-liberationfront-ethiopia-december-2024-accessible Belgian CGRS, Ethiopia: Security Situation in Amhara, May 28, 2026 https://www.cgra.be/sites/default/files/rapporten/coi_focus_ethiopie._veiligheidssituatie_i n_amhara_20260528.pdf Freedom House, Freedom on the Net 2026: Ethiopia https://freedomhouse.org/country/ethiopia/freedom-net/2026 Council on Foreign Relations, Ethiopia Conflict Tracker, updated November 2026 https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/conflict-ethiopia Editorial caution: Figures, battlefield control and responsibility for specific incidents may be disputed or changed. This article distinguishes institutional findings from analysis and proposals. Check sources again immediately before publication. The recommendations are proposals, not claims of agreement among parties. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's ongoing conflict, particularly since Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's rise to power in 2018, reveals deep-rooted issues surrounding political legitimacy and governance. Initially celebrated for reforms and a peace prize for rapprochement with Eritrea, Abiy's administration has systematically dismantled national institutions, favoring Oromo elites and exacerbating ethnic tensions. The resultant violence, particularly against Amhara and Tigrayan communities, has led to accusations of war crimes and ethnic cleansing. Despite the 2022 Pretoria agreement halting major hostilities, underlying disputes remain unresolved, with significant stakeholders excluded from negotiations. The government's intolerance of dissent and reliance on division further complicate peace efforts. To achieve lasting stability, a comprehensive peace process must include accountability, inclusive negotiations, and protections for civilians. Immediate actions should focus on protecting lives, facilitating humanitarian access, and initiating dialogue among all affected parties. Without addressing these foundational issues, Ethiopia's path to peace remains elusive, with the potential for broader regional conflict looming.

Ethiopian News November 20, 2026 Updated: November 20, 2026 U.S. Issues Travel Alert as Border Clashes and Troop Build-Up Heighten Ethiopia-Eritrea War Fears, Reports November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Rising tensions and artillery fire along the border prompt a U.S. travel warning as Ethiopian and Eritrean forces mass near Badme File/SM By Staff Writer (Nairobi, Kenya) — Heavy troop deployments, artillery exchanges, and cross-border clashes along the Ethiopia-Eritrea frontier have raised fears of a wider war, prompting the U.S. Embassy in Ethiopia to issue a security warning to its citizens, according to BBC Amharic and international reports. In a warning issued on Thursday, November 19, 2026, the U.S. Embassy urged Americans to reconsider travel to Ethiopia. The embassy advised against travel to the Tigray, Amhara, and Afar regions—specifically highlighting southern Afar and rural border areas of Tigray—and called on U.S. citizens in those areas to leave while safe to do so. BBC Amharic reported that the alert follows assessments from international outlets, including AFP and Reuters on November 18, 2026, indicating that Ethiopia and Eritrea stand on the brink of war as forces position themselves at close range along the border. Citing the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) and sources linked to armed groups, Reuters reported direct military exchanges in recent days. AFP cited analysts and foreign security sources pointing to heavy weapons attacks, cross-border incursions, and military preparations on the Ethiopian side. ACLED reported that Eritrean troops redeployed to the Badme area last week after pulling back in mid-October, massing soldiers and heavy equipment in Gwal Gemhalo and Simbel. Meanwhile, Ethiopian forces deployed close to the front line and fired heavy artillery toward positions near Badme, a contested flashpoint of the 1998–2000 war. Accounts of the fighting remain disputed. A source close to a pro-government militia in Tigray rejected reports of direct clashes with Eritrean forces. Eritrea’s Minister of Information, Yemane Gebremeskel, dismissed reports of border tensions as Ethiopian ruling-party propaganda without addressing troop deployments or fighting directly. Residents in Tigray’s North West Zone—including in Shiraro, Adi Hageray, and Biyara—told BBC Amharic that fighting involving artillery and drones pushed into rural areas earlier in the month, displacing border residents. Local officials, medical sources, and BBC Amharic accounts also reported that a drone strike in Biyara kebele near Badme on Monday, November 16, 2026, wounded at least four civilians riding in a white Isuzu pickup truck. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated sharply following Ethiopia’s push for sea access, mutual accusations involving armed groups, and severed diplomatic ties. Both governments have traded accusations at the United Nations since hostilities flared again in Tigray in mid-September 2026. __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Join the conversation. The warning, released on November 19, 2026, advises against travel to the Tigray, Amhara, and Afar regions, particularly southern Afar and rural Tigray, urging those already in these areas to leave while it is still safe. Recent reports indicate heavy troop deployments and artillery exchanges, raising fears of a potential war as forces from both nations position themselves near the contested Badme area. The situation has escalated since mid-September 2026, with accusations exchanged between the two governments at the United Nations. Local accounts describe artillery and drone strikes displacing residents, while Eritrean officials have dismissed reports of clashes as propaganda. News November 20, 2026 Updated: November 20, 2026 IFPRI Study Warns El Niño and Global Fuel Shocks Threaten Food Security and Push Millions Toward Poverty in Ethiopia November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Compounding climate pressures and rising fuel prices threaten food security, risking deeper poverty and widespread nutritional deficits by 2027 SM By Staff Writer (Nairobi, Kenya) — Compounding pressures from El Niño and escalating global fuel prices pose severe risks to Ethiopia’s food security heading into 2027, according to an International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) study reported by Addis Maleda . Using the Rural Investment and Policy Analysis (RIAPA) data modeling system, researchers project a measurable decline in domestic agricultural output. This reduction threatens to push 905,000 more citizens into poverty and leave roughly 2.8 million additional people unable to secure adequate nutrition. The study highlights that disruptions from geopolitical conflicts—specifically instability in Iran driving fuel price volatility—and intensifying climate impacts leave Ethiopia’s agrarian economy highly vulnerable. Surging fuel costs have directly raised agricultural input expenses, notably driving up fertilizer prices. This inflation lowers crop yields and reduces purchasing power for both rural and urban households. To prevent a large-scale humanitarian emergency, IFPRI emphasizes the need for urgent policy measures, enhanced early warning systems, and robust social protection frameworks to safeguard vulnerable populations. ethiopia.summary: A recent study by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) highlights the severe threats posed by El Niño and rising global fuel prices to food security in Ethiopia, projecting significant increases in poverty and nutritional deficits by 2027. Utilizing the Rural Investment and Policy Analysis (RIAPA) data modeling system, the research indicates that Ethiopia's agricultural output will decline, potentially pushing an additional 905,000 people into poverty and leaving approximately 2.8 million without adequate nutrition. The study attributes these challenges to geopolitical conflicts, particularly instability in Iran affecting fuel prices, and the escalating impacts of climate change. Rising fuel costs have inflated agricultural input expenses, especially fertilizer prices, leading to lower crop yields and diminished purchasing power for households. To avert a humanitarian crisis, IFPRI calls for urgent policy interventions, improved early warning systems, and stronger social protection measures to support vulnerable populations in Ethiopia.

Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed TPLF, party that parted ways with Ethiopia's ruling party, blocked army movements in and out of Tigray State Ethiopia’s prime minister has ordered a military response to a Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) attack on a military camp in the regional capital of Mekele. Earlier, authorities of the TPLF, a party that parted ways with the country’s ruling party, blocked army movements in and out of Tigray State. Just one week ago, a general newly posted by the federal government to lead the northern division of the army in Tigray was sent back to the capital Addis Ababa upon his arrival in Mekele, the capital of a region whose leaders held elections in defiance of federal authority in August. “I call on the people of Ethiopia to rally behind the army in its military response to the TPLF in Mekele," Premier Abiy Ahmed said, describing them as "rogue." Reports say the Ethiopian army is already attacking TPLF bases in Mekele. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has ordered military action against the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), labeling them as "rogue" rulers following an attack on a military camp in Mekele, the regional capital of Tigray. The TPLF, which has distanced itself from the ruling party, had previously obstructed military movements in and out of the region. This escalation comes after a federal general was sent back to Addis Ababa upon arriving in Mekele, highlighting tensions following the TPLF's defiance of federal authority in August elections. In response to the TPLF's actions, Ahmed has called on the Ethiopian populace to support the military's operations against the TPLF, which reportedly has already begun attacking TPLF bases in Mekele. The situation underscores the ongoing conflict and instability in Ethiopia, particularly in the Tigray region, which has faced significant unrest and military confrontations in recent years.

ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa 20 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has invited African leaders, health experts, and global partners to Addis Ababa for the Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), calling for collective action to build a healthier and more resilient continent. In a video message shared on social media, the Prime Minister announced that Ethiopia will host the conference from November 23 to 27 at the Addis International Convention Center. The event will be co-hosted by Ethiopia and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The conference is expected to bring together heads of state, ministers, researchers, innovators, and development partners to strengthen continental cooperation and advance African-led solutions to public health challenges, he said. PM Abiy said Ethiopia was proud to host the important gathering and looking forward to welcoming leaders, researchers, and partners from across Africa and beyond. The conference provides an important opportunity to unite knowledge, strengthen partnerships, and advance African-led solutions to the continent's health priorities, the Prime Minister underscored. "Together, let us turn shared aspirations into collective action and build a healthier, more resilient Africa," the Prime Minister underscored, adding, "Africa is ready." Held under the theme "Africa's Health Security and Sovereignty," CPHIA 2026 will focus on reducing external dependence in the health sector, strengthening resilient healthcare systems, and advancing African ownership of public health priorities. somalia.title: Somalia must reject Ethiopia’s “necklace of ports” - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia must reject Ethiopia’s “necklace of ports” - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia must reject Ethiopia’s “necklace of ports” Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hussein Soyan Sunday November 22, 2026 Ethiopia’s need for the sea is legitimate, but Somalia’s coastline is not for sale. Proposals for permanent, sovereign zones on Somali soil should be refused, and Somalis must end their divisions before others exploit them. Ethiopia’s case for reliable access to the sea is a serious one. It is a landlocked country of more than 120 million people, and almost all of its trade passes through the ports of its neighbours. Somalia should acknowledge this. Somali ports could serve Ethiopian commerce on fair terms, and both nations would benefit from such an arrangement. The question is not whether Ethiopia should have access to the sea, but on what terms, and on whose land. That question became sharper this month. On 4 November, in a Middle East Eye podcastwith David Hearst, Alexander Rondos, the former EU special representative for the Horn of Africa, set out his view of Ethiopia’s options. He said Ethiopia should seek access “in perpetuity”, including sovereign access: a port area of one or two square kilometres guarded by Ethiopian troops. Ethiopia, he argued, should aim for “a guaranteed necklace of ports” around it; without one, it feels it has “a noose” around its neck. His advice to Addis Ababa was not to settle for the noose but to find the necklace, and he said he had told Ethiopian leaders as much himself. advertisements Somalis should be clear about what this means. A necklace of ports around Ethiopia can only be made from the coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia and Kenya. Each port on it would be a piece of another country placed under Ethiopian sovereignty, guarded by Ethiopian soldiers, with no end date. That is not a trade agreement. It is a transfer of territory, described in the language of diplomacy. Describing dependence on neighbouring ports as a “noose” casts those neighbours as a threat to be escaped rather than partners to be dealt with fairly. Somalia should reject the idea in full. The reason Rondos gave for a sovereign zone is itself revealing. Ethiopia, he said, would need such an area so that it could import “sensitive material” without it being inspected by anyone else. A zone where Somali law does not apply, where Somali officials may not enter and where Somali customs cannot examine what arrives would no longer be Somali in any meaningful sense. Every state insists on knowing what crosses its territory. Commercial goods have nothing to fear from inspection. Cargo that must be hidden from the hostcountry is, by definition, something other than ordinary trade, and it has no place on Somali soil. There is also an obligation that goes beyond national interest. Somalia, like Ethiopia, is a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and the Chemical Weapons Convention. UN Security Council Resolution 1540 requires every state to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and to control the transit of dangerous materials through its territory. A sealed enclave guarded by foreign troops would make it impossible for Somalia to meet those commitments. If anything harmful passed through such a zone, it would be Somalia that answered to the international community, for cargo it had never been permitted to see. Ethiopia has accepted the same treaty obligations and cannot reasonably ask a neighbour to set them aside. A diplomat with Rondos’s long experience of peace and security in the region understands these obligations well. To propose an uninspected sovereign enclave in one of the world’s most fragile regions is not responsible advice, and it should be challenged. Nor is this a theoretical concern. Ethiopia has already pursued similar terms elsewhere. In April, Djibouti’s ports authority said it had offered Ethiopia a 60 per cent share in the port of Tadjoura, and that Ethiopia declined, seeking a corridor on top of the equity stake. In September, President Guelleh formally turned down an Ethiopian proposal for a corridor with extraterritorial rights stretching from the border to Tadjoura, together with an Ethiopian naval base. A majority stake in a working port was not enough for Addis Ababa. It wanted land, extraterritorial rights and a naval presence, which is precisely the necklace Rondos describes. Djibouti was able to refuse because it spoke with a single voice. Somalia should ask whether it could do the same. Its federal government and member states frequently pull in opposite directions; politicians compete for foreign patronage; clan rivalries continue to be turned against the national interest. The memorandum of understanding Ethiopia signed with Somaliland in January 2024, offering sea access in return for recognition, showed how readily a divided country can be negotiated with one region at a time. Ethiopia’s governments have changed many times since the era of Emperor Menelik, but the ambition for a coastline has remained constant. Where a united Djibouti could say no, a fragmented Somalia risks answering with many voices, and there will usually be someone prepared to say yes. This is why the warning matters most to younger Somalis, who will inherit whatever is agreed in their name. They should know this history, follow closely what is being negotiated, and hold every leader, federal and regional, to a clear standard. Ethiopia may have commercial access to Somali ports: open, subject to inspection and governed by Somali law. It may not have sovereign territory, foreign troops or uninspected cargo on the Somali coast, whether by agreement, for any price or in perpetuity. Somalis have united before when their land was under threat. They should not wait for another crisis to do so again. National reconciliation is now a matter of national security. A united Somalia would leave no opening to exploit, and would leave Ethiopia with a single realistic course: a fair commercial partnership that serves both countries and supports lasting stability in the Horn of Africa. __________________________________ Hussein Soyan is a former Somali head of mission to Algeria, and a political analyst, lecturer and social finance expert. somalia.summary: Somalia must firmly reject Ethiopia's proposal for a "necklace of ports," which would effectively transfer Somali territory to Ethiopian control. While Ethiopia's need for sea access is acknowledged, the idea of granting Ethiopia sovereign zones on Somali soil, as suggested by former EU representative Alexander Rondos, poses significant risks. Such zones would allow Ethiopia to operate without Somali oversight, undermining Somalia's sovereignty and international obligations under treaties like the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The article emphasizes that Somalia's fragmented political landscape could lead to dangerous concessions, as seen in Ethiopia's previous negotiations with Djibouti and Somaliland. A united Somalia is essential to prevent exploitation and ensure that any commercial access to Somali ports is governed by Somali law, with proper inspections. The call for national reconciliation is framed as a matter of national security, urging Somalis to unite against external pressures and negotiate fair partnerships that promote stability in the Horn of Africa.

somalia.title: Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 22, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Bitcoin briefly fell below $56,000 on Saturday, Nov. 21, hitting its lowest level in more than two years as a stronger U.S. dollar and uncertainty over American interest rates weighed on cryptocurrency markets. The world's largest cryptocurrency dropped to approximately $55,000 before recovering toward $60,000 later in the day. The decline left Bitcoin more than 50% below its October 2025 peak of over $126,000. advertisements For most Somali households, however, the cryptocurrency selloff has little direct effect on everyday spending. Commerce in Mogadishu, Hargeisa and other major cities relies heavily on U.S. dollars transferred through mobile money services rather than Bitcoin. The more immediate concern is the strengthening U.S. dollar, which can increase the cost of sending remittances for Somali workers earning their incomes in other currencies. Bitcoin's latest decline comes amid growing uncertainty in international financial markets over U.S. interest rates, inflation and the outlook for economic growth. Investors have reassessed expectations for Federal Reserve monetary policy, contributing to a stronger dollar and increasing pressure on risk-sensitive assets, including cryptocurrencies and technology stocks. The U.S. Dollar Index, which measures the dollar against a basket of major currencies, approached 104 during the week, reportedly its highest level in approximately 19 months. A stronger dollar can make dollar-denominated investments more expensive for international investors, while expectations of higher interest rates can increase the attractiveness of cash and government bonds relative to speculative assets. Bitcoin has also faced selling pressure from institutional investors, including funds holding the cryptocurrency through exchange-traded products. Institutional selling, combined with the forced liquidation of leveraged trading positions, has contributed to sharp price movements. The latest selloff highlights Bitcoin's continued vulnerability to changes in global financial conditions, despite its frequent promotion as a digital alternative to traditional stores of value. Somalia is among the economies most dependent on remittances from citizens living and working abroad. According to the Central Bank of Somalia's 2025 annual report, individual remittances reached $3.13 billion, up from $2.72 billion in 2024. These transfers represented approximately 24% of Somalia's gross domestic product in 2025, demonstrating their importance to household consumption and economic stability. Remittances help families pay for food, housing, education, healthcare and other basic necessities. Unlike countries where households primarily use domestic currencies, Somalia's economy is heavily dollarized. Many consumers receive, store and spend U.S. dollars through mobile money platforms such as EVC Plus, Zaad and Sahal. This system means changes in the dollar's international value can directly affect the cost of remittances for Somali workers living abroad. For example, a Somali worker in London earning British pounds must convert those earnings into U.S. dollars before sending money home. If the pound falls from $1.35 to $1.31, sending $200 would cost approximately £153 instead of £148, excluding transfer fees. The difference may appear modest for a single transaction, but repeated monthly transfers can become more expensive for workers supporting relatives in Somalia. The same pressure affects Somali workers earning euros, Canadian dollars and other currencies that weaken against the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar does not necessarily reduce the amount received by a family in Somalia if the sender continues transferring the same dollar amount. Instead, it increases the cost for senders earning weaker foreign currencies. Somalia's reliance on the U.S. dollar provides some protection against exchange-rate instability compared with economies that depend on rapidly depreciating domestic currencies. However, dollarization does not shield households from inflation or increases in international commodity prices. Somalia imports substantial quantities of food, fuel, construction materials and manufactured goods, making domestic prices sensitive to changes in global supply chains, transportation costs and commodity markets. Rising energy prices, shipping disruptions and supply shortages can increase the cost of imported products, even when transactions are conducted in dollars. A stronger dollar can also reduce the dollar cost of goods priced in weaker foreign currencies, meaning its effect on Somalia's import bill depends on the product, supplier and market conditions. According to the International Monetary Fund's October 2026 assessment, Somalia's inflation rate is projected to reach 6.5% in 2026. Higher living costs, combined with pressure on remittance senders abroad, could place additional financial strain on households already facing economic and humanitarian challenges. Families that depend on regular financial assistance from relatives overseas may be particularly vulnerable if senders reduce the frequency or value of transfers because of unfavorable exchange rates. Although Bitcoin remains a speculative investment for many traders, dollar-pegged stablecoins such as USDT serve a different purpose. Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a value linked to an underlying asset, usually the U.S. dollar. Some Somali freelancers and cross-border traders use stablecoins to transfer funds internationally without relying entirely on traditional banking channels. However, stablecoins carry their own risks, including issuer, liquidity, regulatory and technical risks, and their dollar pegs are not guaranteed. For most Somali households, conventional remittance companies and mobile money services remain more relevant than cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin's decline illustrates how global financial markets react to changing expectations about interest rates, inflation and the strength of the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar can increase the international purchasing power of dollar holdings, but it can also make dollar-denominated remittances more expensive for relatives earning income in other currencies. This decline left Bitcoin over 50% lower than its peak in October 2025. While the cryptocurrency's volatility impacts global markets, it has minimal direct effects on everyday spending in Somalia, where commerce relies more on U.S. dollars transferred via mobile money services. The strengthening dollar increases remittance costs for Somali workers earning in weaker currencies, which can strain families dependent on these funds. somalia.title: Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea reaffirm support for Somalia's unity, reject parallel entities - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea reaffirm support for Somalia's unity, reject parallel entities - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME POLITICS Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea reaffirm support for Somalia's unity, reject parallel entities Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 22, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — The foreign ministers of Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea have reaffirmed their support for Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity, rejecting the establishment of parallel political entities while calling for closer regional cooperation on Red Sea security. The three ministers met Saturday, Nov. 21, on the sidelines of the sixth Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development in Egypt, where they discussed regional security challenges, maritime navigation and political cooperation among countries in the Horn of Africa. advertisements According to a statement from Egypt's Foreign Ministry, the meeting brought together Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieddin Salem and Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh. The ministers emphasized the importance of respecting Somalia's unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity and expressed opposition to the establishment of parallel entities that could undermine the country's state institutions. The statement did not identify any specific administration or political group in connection with its rejection of parallel entities. The ministers also agreed to strengthen consultation and coordination on issues of mutual concern, building on agreements reached during a four-country summit held in Egypt last month. The October summit in New Alamein brought together the leaders of Egypt, Somalia and Eritrea, along with Sudan's military leader, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, to discuss security, regional cooperation and political developments in the Horn of Africa. During Saturday's meeting, Abdelatty said Egypt would brief Somalia on the discussions as part of efforts to maintain coordination among the four countries. The ministers reaffirmed their commitment to the outcomes of the Alamein summit, emphasizing the importance of closer cooperation to address regional security threats and protect national sovereignty. They also discussed developments in the Red Sea, calling for stronger cooperation to maintain maritime security, protect international shipping routes and ensure freedom of navigation. The ministers stressed that responsibility for governing the Red Sea and safeguarding its security should rest with countries bordering the waterway. Their position reflects growing regional discussions over the security of the Red Sea, a strategically important shipping corridor connecting international trade routes through the Suez Canal and the Gulf of Aden. The three ministers also reaffirmed their support for Sudan's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity amid the country's continuing conflict. They emphasized the importance of preserving Sudan's national institutions and rejected the involvement of armed militias and the provision of weapons to such groups from foreign sources. The ministers similarly expressed support for Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity. They opposed unilateral measures affecting regional security and water resources, stressing that disputes should be addressed through consultation and respect for international law. The discussions also emphasized the principle of noninterference in the internal affairs of states, with the three countries agreeing to maintain coordination aimed at strengthening regional stability and development. Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea have increased diplomatic consultations in recent months amid security and political challenges affecting the Horn of Africa and Red Sea region. The delegation was led by Mohamed Ghrab, Director of Laboratories at Sonatrach’s Exploration and Production Directorate, according to a statement from the Somali National News Agency. The meeting followed a series of engagements between Sonatrach and Somali petroleum officials in Mogadishu over the past week, including a visit to the national oil depot at the Port of Mogadishu and technical discussions with the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources. A Relationship Built on Training and Expertise The Sonatrach visit is the most visible outcome of a strategic partnership agreement signed during President Mohamud’s visit to Algeria in 2025, which covered cooperation in oil, gas, and minerals. In the months since, the relationship has focused primarily on capacity building rather than direct investment. During talks at the Port of Mogadishu on November 16, Sonatrach representatives expressed readiness to share technical expertise in exploration, production, and refining, and to support the training of Somali petroleum engineers. Deputy Petroleum Minister Abdiwahab Abdi Omar Ananug described the offer in practical terms, saying that Somalia needs partners who teach it to produce its own resources rather than those who simply provide finished products, as FTL Somalia reported . Algeria has also offered 500 scholarships to Somali students, including in petroleum engineering, a commitment made during the 2025 presidential visit. The Somali Petroleum Authority has indicated that further announcements are expected, though no details have been disclosed. No Exploration Deal Yet Despite the high-level meeting at Villa Somalia, no agreement has been announced under which Sonatrach would conduct oil exploration or make direct investments in Somalia. The company’s offers so far are limited to technical assistance and training. Somali officials have not disclosed a timeline for when Sonatrach might move from advisory support to operational activity. Sonatrach is Africa’s largest oil and gas company, and Algeria has positioned itself as a partner for Somalia’s emerging hydrocarbons sector. The relationship also carries diplomatic weight: Algeria has been a vocal supporter of Somalia’s territorial integrity and has publicly opposed Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, as FTL Somalia reported . FTL Critical Note The Sonatrach delegation’s visit to Villa Somalia is a signal of deepening political ties between Mogadishu and Algiers, but it is not yet an oil deal. What Somalia has secured from Algeria is training, scholarships, and technical advice. What it has not secured is a commitment from Sonatrach to explore, drill, or invest. The distinction matters. Somalia’s hydrocarbons sector has attracted a series of agreements in recent years, but production remains elusive. The government has signed deals with Turkish Petroleum, Coastline Exploration, and other firms, yet no commercial oil has been exported. In April, the government issued warnings to foreign oil companies demanding they begin exploration or face license revocation, a sign of frustration with the gap between signed contracts and tangible activity. Sonatrach’s arrival adds a new partner to the list, but it does not change the fundamental challenge: Somalia’s oil potential is unproven, its regulatory framework is contested, and the Federal Government’s authority over resource deals is disputed by regional administrations. Algeria’s offer of training is valuable, and the scholarships for Somali students are a genuine investment in human capital. But training engineers is not the same as building an oil industry. Until Sonatrach or another company commits to drilling and the legal and political disputes over resource governance are resolved, Somalia’s oil sector will remain what it has been for years: a promise that has yet to be tested. The meeting, held at the presidential palace, followed previous engagements between Sonatrach and Somali officials, including technical discussions and a visit to Mogadishu's national oil depot. somalia.title: Somalia Launches Digital Registry for Private Security Companies, Bans Soldiers from Working for Firms - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Somalia Launches Digital Registry for Private Security Companies, Bans Soldiers from Working for Firms - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Nationwide Somalia Launches Digital Registry for Private Security Companies, Bans Soldiers from Working for Firms November 22, 2026 4 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Minister of Internal Security, Abdullahi Sheikh Ismail (Fartaag), officially launched a new system on Saturday for registering, managing, and training private security companies and their personnel, part of an effort to bring a largely unregulated sector under closer government oversight. The framework focuses on three areas: registration and management of private security firms, training and professional development for security guards, and improving the quality and professionalism of private security services, according to a ministry announcement. The launch is part of the Ministry of Internal Security’s broader push to modernize how private security companies are managed and to strengthen oversight and accountability mechanisms. Soldiers Barred from Private Security Work Alongside the registration system, the ministry announced a prohibition on serving members of Somalia’s security forces working for private security companies. Abbas Ali Hussein, Director of the Security Department at the Ministry, said private firms must operate independently of state forces, with separate weapons, equipment, and personnel. “Any soldier serving in the Federal Government of Somalia is not entitled to work for a private security company. We want private security companies to operate separately, with their own weapons, equipment and everything they use,” Hussein said. The new system also includes a digital weapons registry, allowing the government to monitor and manage firearms held by private security firms. The ministry said companies are now required to comply with the registration framework effective immediately. A Sector Long in Need of Regulation The move follows a Cabinet decision in May 2026 approving a Regulation on Private Security Services, presented by the Ministry of Internal Security and chaired by Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre. The regulation was designed to address a sector that has expanded rapidly in Mogadishu and other urban centers, where businesses, NGOs, and wealthy individuals rely on private guards for protection. The United Nations Working Group on the use of mercenaries has previously noted that Somalia’s regulatory structure for private military and security companies was “minimal and requires significant improvements.” The Working Group recommended that any licensing regime include ongoing monitoring, sufficient resources, and mechanisms for accountability in cases of human rights violations. Private security services have become an integral part of Mogadishu’s security landscape. In recent years, the capital has seen expanded use of private guards for businesses, alongside municipal security cameras and community policing initiatives, as FTL Somalia reported in its coverage of security cooperation with international partners. FTL Critical Note The launch of a registration and oversight system for private security companies is a necessary step. For years, armed guards employed by private firms have operated in a regulatory vacuum, with unclear lines of accountability, inconsistent training standards, and weapons that were not systematically tracked. The decision to bar serving soldiers from moonlighting as private guards addresses a particularly problematic overlap: when state security personnel work for private companies, the distinction between public authority and commercial protection blurs. But a registry is only as effective as its enforcement. The ministry has announced a system; it has not explained how it will verify compliance, what penalties will apply to companies that fail to register, or how it will monitor the estimated thousands of guards already working in the capital. The digital weapons registry is a useful tool, but it depends on companies accurately reporting their arsenals, a requirement that may be difficult to enforce in a sector where informal arrangements have long been the norm. The deeper question is whether regulation will improve accountability or simply add a layer of fees and paperwork for companies that already operate with minimal oversight. The UN Working Group’s recommendation for ongoing monitoring, not just one-time registration, is the right standard. Whether the ministry has the capacity and political will to meet it remains to be seen. A system that registers companies but does not inspect them, or that records weapons but does not trace them, will not deliver the accountability the sector needs. The initiative, announced by Minister of Internal Security Abdullahi Sheikh Ismail, focuses on the registration, management, and training of private security personnel to enhance professionalism and accountability. A significant aspect of this new framework is the prohibition of active soldiers from working for private security firms, ensuring a clear separation between state forces and private entities. The Ministry emphasizes that private security companies must operate independently, with their own resources. Additionally, a digital weapons registry will help monitor firearms held by these firms.
